new_statements.quote: Tolkien described the basic Sindarin stress patterns in The Lord of the Rings Appendix E (LotR/1116), and they are essentially the same as for Quenya (and Latin): stress falls on heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, except (a) it cannot fall on the last syllable of polysyllables and (b) cannot be further back than the third-to-last syllable. A syllable is “light” if it has a short vowel followed by no more than one consonant; it is “heavy” if it has a long vowel, a diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant. [Tolkien's wording per Derdzinski:] In words of two syllables it falls on the first syllable ... In longer words it falls on the last syllable but one, where that contains a long vowel, a diphthong, or a vowel followed by two (or more) consonants ... Where the last syllable but one contains a short vowel followed by only one (or no) consonant, the stress falls on the syllable before it, the third from the end

new_statements.rule_in_words: Latin-type weight-sensitive stress within a three-syllable right-edge window: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; in longer words the penult is stressed if heavy (long vowel, diphthong, or vowel followed by two or more consonants), otherwise the antepenult. Final syllables of polysyllables are never stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Tolkien never described secondary stress for Sindarin. Eldamo infers from the metre of A Elbereth Gilthoniel and Lúthien's Song (read as iambic tetrameter) that secondary stress falls on alternating syllables before and after the main stress (e.g. a Él|berèth | Gilthó|nièl), with the caveat that the sample is small. Jallings defines a secondary-stress notation but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Tolkien's hedge 'in practically all cases' for disyllables (LotR/1116). Digraphs th, ch, dh are single consonants and do not make a syllable heavy (linnathon = Linguistics Library-na-thon); ph between vowels = long [ff] and does make the penult heavy (Orophin = o-ROF-fin); intervocalic m derived from mb/mm counts as a long consonant for stress though pronounced single (Turamarth = tu-RA-marth; Tolkien LotR/1115). Diphthongs ae, ui may count as two syllables metrically (RGEO/63). Early Gnomish (GG/13) had different accentual rules.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms (names and lexical words). Eldamo adds that in connected speech 'minor' monosyllables (prepositions, short adverbs) may be unstressed, and that pseudo-compounds like palan-díriel may carry a single primary stress; Derdzinski's examples are isolated names.
new_statements.identity_note: Sindarin is a constructed language (Tolkien); Glottolog lists no descriptive references. The stress rule is Tolkien's Appendix E rule for 'the Eldarin languages concerned', i.e. identical for Quenya (quen1234) and Sindarin; the saved Eldamo entry describes Tolkien's mature ('classical') Sindarin, the same variety Salo 2004 describes. Earlier conceptual stages (Gnomish/Goldogrin 1917, 'Noldorin' of the 1930s Etymologies) are not the same variety and Eldamo notes the Gnomish accent rules differed. The RealElvish.net page describes neo-Sindarin (fan usage) but states the same rule.

sources.note: Latin-type weight rule after Tolkien Appendix E: stress on the heavy syllable nearest the end, never final in polysyllables, never further back than antepenult; light = short V + <=1 C, heavy = long V, diphthong, or short V + 2+ C; disyllables initial; digraphs th/ch/dh count as one C, ph = long ff counts heavy, medial m (< mb) counts long for stress; secondary stress not described by Tolkien, metrical analysis of two poems suggests alternating secondary stress; minor monosyllables may be unstressed in the sentence.

sources.note: Quotes Tolkien's Appendix E rule near-verbatim: two-syllable words stressed on first syllable; longer words on the last syllable but one if it has a long vowel, diphthong or vowel + 2+ consonants, otherwise on the third from the end (cf. LotR Appendix E).

sources.note: Pedagogical (neo-Sindarin) rule: look at the last three syllables; words of 1-3 syllables stress the first; longer words the 3rd from the end, unless the 2nd-to-last has an accented (long) vowel, a diphthong (ae ai au aw ei oe ui) or ends in 2+ consonants (ch dh th count as one), in which case it takes the stress; defines primary and secondary stress notation but gives no secondary-stress rule.
